clinicalPearls: An aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) is the commonest congenital aortic arch anomaly, arising as the last branch of a left-sided arch and coursing behind the oesophagus.
It is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, but its retro-oesophageal course can produce dysphagia lusoria, typically in adults as the vessel stiffens or becomes aneurysmal.
Compression of the trachea may cause stridor or dyspnoea, more often in infants than in adults.
The origin is frequently dilated as a Kommerell diverticulum, which carries a risk of aneurysm formation, dissection and rupture.
An aberrant right subclavian is associated with an absent (non-recurrent) right laryngeal nerve, a crucial consideration during thyroid and neck surgery to avoid nerve injury.
A barium swallow shows a characteristic oblique posterior indentation on the oesophagus, and CT or MR angiography confirms the vessel and any diverticulum.
In isolation it does not form a complete ring, whereas an aberrant left subclavian with a right arch and left ligamentum does.
Asymptomatic cases are observed, while symptomatic dysphagia or an enlarging diverticulum warrants surgical reimplantation or bypass with division of the aberrant vessel.
reference.pathophysiology: The anomaly results from abnormal regression of the embryonic aortic arch system. For an aberrant right subclavian artery, the right fourth arch and proximal right dorsal aorta regress abnormally while a distal segment of the right dorsal aorta persists, so the right subclavian arises as the most distal branch of the left arch and must cross the midline behind the oesophagus to reach the right arm. This retro-oesophageal course places the vessel against the posterior oesophageal wall; in childhood the pliable artery rarely causes symptoms, but with ageing, atherosclerosis and dilatation of the Kommerell diverticulum the vessel becomes rigid and may indent the oesophagus sufficiently to impair swallowing.
additionalDifferentials: Achalasia and other oesophageal motility disorders
Oesophageal or mediastinal neoplasm causing extrinsic compression
Double aortic arch or other complete vascular ring
Right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian artery
additionalInvestigations: CT angiography of the aortic arch
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude mucosal disease
Oesophageal manometry if a motility disorder is suspected
Transthoracic echocardiography for associated cardiac anomalies
Genetic evaluation given associations with trisomy 21 and 22q11.2 deletion
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dysphagia or weight loss, prompting exclusion of malignancy
An aneurysmal Kommerell diverticulum or signs of dissection
Stridor or respiratory distress in an infant
reference.prognosis: The great majority of patients remain asymptomatic with a normal life expectancy; symptomatic disease and an aneurysmal diverticulum have good outcomes after appropriate surgical repair.
pitfalls: Attributing dysphagia to the anomaly without excluding a coexisting oesophageal malignancy.
Inadvertent injury to a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery when the anomaly is unrecognised.
Overlooking an aneurysmal Kommerell diverticulum that requires treatment.
Confusing an isolated aberrant subclavian (no ring) with a complete vascular ring.
Assuming that symptoms in an infant simply represent benign gastro-oesophageal reflux.
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
management: Manage asymptomatic incidental cases conservatively with reassurance and no intervention
Offer dietary modification with softer textures and careful chewing for mild dysphagia lusoria before considering intervention
Refer symptomatic dysphagia or tracheal compression for surgical repair, with division of the aberrant artery and reimplantation or transposition and repair of any associated Kommerell diverticulum
Repair a Kommerell diverticulum that is aneurysmal or enlarging because of the risk of dissection and rupture
Surveil a known diverticulum with periodic CT or MR angiography for growth
Alert the surgical team to the associated non-recurrent laryngeal nerve during thyroid or neck surgery to avoid nerve injury
